answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: The first sentence of Pride and Prejudice, published in three volumes by T. Egerton in 1813. Our wording matches the first edition exactly, comma after “fortune” included — a comma most modern reprints, including the Project Gutenberg ↗ text, leave out. The sentence is not a statement of Austen’s belief: the second paragraph immediately turns it round to mean the opposite.

source.heading: The opening of the novel

Volume I, chapter I — the first sentence
“By the author of Sense and Sensibility” — Austen was not named

source.excerpt:
It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.

However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered as the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters.
trail: Against the first edition — volume I of the T. Egerton first edition of 1813 ↗ opens with this sentence, and a second scan ↗ of the same edition reads identically: “a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife”, with the comma after “fortune”.

The comma is usually lost — the Project Gutenberg text ↗ reproduces the illustrated 1894 George Allen edition, which prints “a good fortune must be in want of a wife” with no comma. Both readings are in circulation; ours is the 1813 one.

Anonymous on publication — the title page credits “the author of Sense and Sensibility” rather than Austen, as the first-edition scan shows; Wikipedia’s article on Jane Austen ↗ records that her novels were published anonymously in her lifetime.
Public domain — an 1813 publication, so free of copyright in the United States. Full text at Wikisource ↗ and Project Gutenberg ↗.
source.excerptNote: The first two paragraphs, from the 1813 first edition. The second is what makes the first ironic: the “universally acknowledged truth” turns out to be held entirely by the families doing the acquiring.

source.rightsNote: First published by T. Egerton in 1813, well before the 1931 United States public-domain cutoff, so the text is free to quote, reprint, translate and adapt. A modern edition can only claim its own added material — introduction, notes, and the editorial punctuation that produced the comma-free version of this very sentence.

author.name: Jane Austen
author.heading: About Jane Austen
author.bio: Jane Austen wrote an early version of Pride and Prejudice in the 1790s as First Impressions; a publisher turned it down unseen, and it appeared, heavily revised, in 1813. She published anonymously throughout her life. Her characteristic move is the sentence that says one thing and means its opposite, and she put the clearest example of it first, where nobody could miss it.

misattribution.heading: Rightly credited — routinely misread
misattribution.intro: Nobody disputes that Austen wrote this. Two things do go wrong: the punctuation, and the assumption that the sentence means what it says.

items.who: “a good fortune must be in want of a wife”
items.why: The comma after “fortune” is in the 1813 first edition ↗ and absent from the 1894 George Allen text that Project Gutenberg ↗ reproduces — which is why both versions circulate.

items.who: The sentence as a sincere maxim
items.why: The next paragraph makes it ironic: the “truth” is held by the neighbourhood families, who treat any rich newcomer as “the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters”.

items.who: The narrator, not Jane Austen in person
items.why: Austen’s narrator adopts the opinions of the society being described in order to expose them. Quoting the line as her own view of marriage reverses its point.

misattribution.truthLine: Austen’s, word for word — and the 1813 first edition ↗ settles the comma.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: It is probably the most familiar opening sentence in English, and it works by pretending to be a proverb. A universal truth is announced, in the flattest possible register, and then quietly handed over to the people who actually believe it.

By the second paragraph the “truth” has been relocated into the minds of the surrounding families, who treat an eligible man as property to be allocated. Nothing has been argued; the sentence has simply been turned inside out.
detailsBody: Austen drafted the novel as First Impressions between 1796 and 1797. Her father offered it to the publisher Thomas Cadell, who declined it without reading it. She revised it substantially and it was published by T. Egerton in January 1813, in three volumes, credited only to “the author of Sense and Sensibility”.

The irony of the opening is set up immediately by the scene that follows: Mrs Bennet arrives with news that Netherfield Park is let at last, and spends the rest of the chapter demonstrating the exact assumption the first sentence has just described.
context.pull: A universal truth that turns out to be held by the neighbours.

sourcesVerified.claim: Volume I of the 1813 T. Egerton first edition opens "It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife." — with a comma after "fortune".
A second scan of the 1813 first edition reads identically, confirming the comma after "fortune".
The Project Gutenberg text (the 1894 George Allen edition) prints the opening sentence without a comma after "fortune".
Pride and Prejudice was first published in 1813 by T. Egerton.
Jane Austen lived 1775-1817 and was an English novelist.
Wikipedia’s Jane Austen article states that Sense and Sensibility (1811) and Pride and Prejudice (1813) were published anonymously.
